'''Frederic Middlebrook Richards''' (August 19, 1925 – January 11, 2009), commonly referred to as '''Fred Richards''', was an American [[biochemist]] and [[biophysics|biophysicist]] known for solving the pioneering [[crystallography|crystal structure]] of the [[ribonuclease S]] [[enzyme]] in 1967 and for defining the concept of [[solvent-accessible surface]]. He contributed many key experimental and theoretical results and developed new methods, garnering over 20,000 journal citations in several quite distinct research areas.  In addition to the protein crystallography and biochemistry of ribonuclease S, these included solvent accessibility and internal packing of proteins, the first side-chain [[rotamer]] library, high-pressure crystallography, new types of chemical tags such as [[biotin]]/[[avidin]], the [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] (NMR) [[chemical shift]] index, and structural and biophysical characterization of the effects of [[mutations]].

Richards spent his entire academic research career at [[Yale University]], where he became [[Sterling Professor]] of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry in the department that he created and chaired, "one of the major centers in the world for the study of biophysics and structural biology".<ref name="Steitz">{{cite journal| author=Steitz, TA| title=Retrospective. Frederic M. Richards (1925–2009)| journal=Science| year=2009| volume=323| page=1181| pmid=19251620| doi=10.1126/science.1171157| issue=5918| s2cid=29807609| author-link=Thomas A. Steitz}}</ref> He was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] USA and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and received many other scientific awards. He served as head of the [[Jane Coffin Childs Memorial Fund for Medical Research]] and was elected as president both of the American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (ASBMB) and of the [[Biophysical Society]].

[[Image:RibonucleaseS ribbon drawing scratchboard.png|thumb|right| 3D structure of ribonuclease S, drawn as the frontispiece for an early review on protein structure<ref name="anatax">{{cite book | last = Richardson | first = JS | author-link = Jane S. Richardson |  year = 1981 | title = The Anatomy and Taxonomy of Proteins | journal = Advances in Protein Chemistry | volume = 34 | pages = 167–339 [http://kinemage.biochem.duke.edu/teaching/Anatax/] | doi = 10.1016/S0065-3233(08)60520-3 | pmid=7020376| isbn = 9780120342341 }}</ref>]]

==Personal biography==
Richards was born on August 19, 1925, in [[New York City]] to George H. Richards and Marianna Middlebrook Richards. Both parents were from old [[New England]] families who had settled in [[Fairfield, Connecticut|Fairfield]] and [[New London, Connecticut]], in the 1600s.  The family usually spent summers in [[Connecticut]], giving Richards an early affinity for the area which continued through his career at [[Yale University]].<ref name="Fred"/> He had two older sisters, Marianna and Sarah. Marianna became a biochemist, and was a significant role model for Fred, who delighted in the smells and explosions produced by chemistry sets in that era.<ref name="Lim">{{cite journal | author=Lim WA| title=Frederic M Richards 1925–2009| journal=Nature Structural & Molecular Biology |year=2009 |volume=16 |pages=230–232 |pmid=19259121 |doi=10.1038/nsmb0309-230 | issue=3| s2cid=20332421|doi-access=free }}</ref> He attended high school at [[Phillips Exeter Academy]], and later recalled that "the excellent science department even permitted certain students the unsupervised run of the laboratories outside of class hours. This attitude played a strong role... in cementing our commitment to scientific careers."<ref name="Fred"/> He learned [[glassblowing]] and [[electronics]] there, and tried to measure the [[universal gravitational constant]] using 100-pound cannonballs.<ref name="Fred"/>

With strong science interests, Richards thwarted his family's expectations by choosing MIT ([[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]) rather than Yale for college in 1943, majoring in chemistry. His undergraduate time was interrupted by two years in the army, which he described as "uneventful".<ref name="Fred"/> He then joined the Biochemistry department at [[Harvard Medical School]] and the lab of Barbara Low. She had worked with [[Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin]] to solve the x-ray crystal structure of [[penicillin]], and was later active in protein crystallography. The [[phase problem]] had not yet been solved to allow determination of protein structure, so his Ph.D. thesis (completed in 1952) studied the density and solvent content in crystals to help determine very accurate [[molecular weight]]s for proteins. In 1954 he went to the [[Carlsberg Laboratory]] in Copenhagen to do postdoctoral research with [[Kaj Ulrik Linderstrøm-Lang|Kaj Linderstrøm-Lang]], where he started his classic work on the ribonuclease enzyme.<ref name="Lim"/> He also absorbed the scientific and mentorship style of Lang, who Richards called "a delightful individual, full of fun and jokes as well as science" exemplifying "simple, inexpensive, ingenious, and insightful experiments".<ref name="Carlsberg"/> In 1955 Richards joined the faculty at Yale University, where he stayed for the rest of his career.

[[Image:FMRichards & SWR MtWashington.jpg|thumb|right| Sally and Fred Richards near the top of Mt Washington, around 1980]]
Richards was an avid and enthusiastic sailor. In addition to sailing on [[Long Island Sound]], he voyaged north along the Canadian coast, south to Bermuda, and even across the Atlantic several times with a small crew of family and friends.<ref name="Steitz"/><ref name="Rose">{{cite journal | author=Rose GD |title=In Memoriam: Frederic M. Richards (1925–2009) |year=2009 |journal=Proteins |volume=75 |pages=535–539 |pmid=19226638 |doi=10.1002/prot.22400 |issue=3|s2cid=29462414 }}</ref> He and his wife had sailboats (Hekla 1 and 2) and an outboard-motor utility boat known as "Sally's Baage"<ref name="GLCT2011"/> (the spelling presumably a comment on her Maine accent), which he had built himself.<ref name="Rose"/>  [[Christian B. Anfinsen|Chris Anfinsen]], Richards's friend and his colleague as editors of Advances in Protein Chemistry<ref name="Rose"/> and who recommended the Carlsberg Lab to him,<ref name="Fred"/> was also an avid sailor, and they sometimes joined forces.<ref name="Rose"/>  [[Wendell Lim]] wrote that, "a dedicated sailor since childhood, Fred almost always took a month off each summer to captain a major sailing excursion, returning to lab afterwards refreshed and ready to work. His sailing adventures included several transatlantic voyages. He was also an avid [[ice hockey]] player."<ref name="Lim"/>

Richards lived in [[Guilford, Connecticut]], a coastal town about 10 miles east of [[New Haven, Connecticut|New Haven]], situated between the Metacomet Ridge and Long Island Sound. Fred was married twice, to Heidi Clark Richards, daughter of biochemist [[Hans Thacher Clarke|Hans Clarke]],<ref name="blog">{{cite web|url=https://fredericmrichards.blogspot.com/|title=Frederic M. Richards|access-date=2009-01-14}}</ref><ref name="Staros"/> and in 1959 to Sarah (Sally) Wheatland Richards, a marine biologist.<ref name="GLCT2011"/> He had three children – Sarah, Ruth, and George – and four grandchildren.<ref name="GLCT2011"/>  His daughter Sarah described him as "a lifelong scientist and sailor.... His main loves were his scientific work which he finished at Yale University, sailing, working in his shop, and helping in the community."<ref name="blog"/> Fred and Sally were a major presence in local land conservation efforts, both on committees and in working projects out on the land and water.<ref name="GLCT2011">{{cite web |url=http://guilfordlandtrust.org/wordpress/2011/04/sally-richards-remembered#more-2824 |title=Sally Richards Remembered |publisher=Guilford Land Conservation Trust |access-date=July 9, 2012}}</ref><ref name="GLCT2010">{{cite web |url=http://guilfordlandtrust.org/wordpress/2010/03/an-incomparable-couple#more-883 |title=An Incomparable Couple |publisher=Guilford Land Conservation Trust |access-date=July 9, 2012}}</ref> He donated a 41-acre shoreline property to the Yale Peabody Museum Natural Areas, which they described as "one of the few natural forest areas left in the state." The property now has long-term protection for use in biological and geological research.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.peabody.yale.edu/collections/facilities |title=Yale Peabody Museum Natural areas: Richards property |date=4 November 2010 |publisher=Yale Peabody Museum |access-date=July 10, 2012}}</ref>

==Research career==

===Two-component ribonuclease S system===
On December 2, 1957, at Yale University, Richards performed a simple experiment on the protein [[Ribonuclease A]] (RNase A) that helped change the scientific community's view of the physical nature of [[protein]] molecules.<ref name="Fred"/> Using a particular [[protease]] ([[Subtilisin]]), RNase A was converted into a split protein ([[Ribonuclease S|RNase S]]), which is composed of two parts called S-peptide and S-protein ({{harvnb|Richards|Vithayathil|1959}}). Richards had developed that cleavage system as a postdoc at the [[Carlsberg Laboratory]] in Copenhagen, Denmark, using purified ribonuclease protein that had been donated to [[Christian Anfinsen]] by the Armour Company and that Anfinsen shared with Richards and other researchers.<ref name="Steitz"/><ref name="Carlsberg"/> Richards found that, when separated, S-protein and S-peptide had no RNase activity, but that the RNase enzymatic activity was restored when the parts were recombined in the test tube.<ref>{{cite journal |author= Richards FM |title=On the enzymic activity of subtilisin-modified ribonuclease |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=44|issue=2 | pages =162–166 |year=1958 |pmid=16590160 |pmc=335382 |doi=10.1073/pnas.44.2.162|bibcode = 1958PNAS...44..162R |doi-access=free }}</ref> In an autobiographical piece, Richards wrote that "this discovery came as a surprise to the scientific community at that time.... In retrospect, this may have been the high point of my career in terms of excitement."<ref name="Fred">{{cite journal| author=Richards FM| title=Whatever Happened to the Fun? An Autobiographical Investigation| journal=Annual Review of Biophysics and Biomolecular Structure| volume=26| pages=1–25| year=1997| doi=10.1146/annurev.biophys.26.1.1| pmid=9241411}}</ref> This experiment showed that proteins maintain 3-dimensional order and tight [[Molecular binding|binding]] between their interacting parts and that the structural information is inherent in the protein itself, foreshadowing both Anfinsen's later work showing that sequence determines structure<ref name="Fox">{{cite journal | author=Fox RO| title=Obituary: Frederic Richards (1925–2009)| journal=Nature| volume=457| page=976| pmid=19225517| doi=10.1038/457976a| issue=7232|date=February 2009|bibcode = 2009Natur.457..976F | s2cid=4422217| doi-access=free}}</ref> and also the idea that [[hormones]] or other small molecules can bind tightly and specifically to proteins,<ref name="Fred"/> a concept basic to how [[pharmaceutical industry|pharmaceutical companies]] design drugs today. Two years later, the protein structure of [[myoglobin]] confirmed such specific 3D relationships.<ref>{{cite journal| author=[[John Kendrew|Kendrew JC]], [[Richard E. Dickerson|Dickerson RE]], Strandberg BE, Hart RG, Davies DR, [[David Chilton Phillips|Phillips DC]], Shore VC| year=1960 |title=Structure of myoglobin: a three-dimensional Fourier synthesis at 2 Å. resolution |journal=Nature| volume=185 |issue=4711 | pages=422–427 |doi=10.1038/185422a0 |bibcode=1960Natur.185..422K | pmid=18990802| s2cid=4167651 }}</ref>  Later, with Marilyn Doscher and Flo Quiocho, Richards demonstrated that ribonuclease S as well as carboxypeptidase were enzymatically active in the crystals, important evidence to silence doubts that the [[Protein structure|conformations of proteins]] in crystals are directly relevant to their biological activity in cells.<ref name="Lim"/><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Doscher MS, Richards FM | year=1963| title=The activity of an enzyme in the crystalline state: Ribonuclease-S| journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry| volume=238| issue=7| pages=2399–2406| doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(19)67984-6| doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Quiocho FA, Richards FM | year=1964 |title=Intermolecular cross linking of a protein in the crystalline state: carboxypeptidase-a | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America| volume= 52 |issue=3 |pages=833–839 |pmid=14212562 |pmc=300354 |doi=10.1073/pnas.52.3.833|bibcode = 1964PNAS...52..833Q | doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Ribonuclease crystal structure===
[[Image:1rns supr on 7rsa.jpg|thumb|right| Ribonuclease S superimposed on the uncleaved ribonuclease A, showing match of overall fold and of His 12 and His 119 (hotpink) at the active site]]
Along with colleague Harold W. Wyckoff, who had worked on early research toward the myoglobin structure,<ref>{{cite journal| author=Bodo G, Dintzis HM, [[John Kendrew|Kendrew JC]], Wyckoff HW| title= The crystal structure of myoglobin. V. A low resolution three-dimensional Fourier synthesis of sperm-whale myoglobin crystals| journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society A | volume=253 |issue=1272 | year=1959| pages=70–102 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1959.0179|bibcode = 1959RSPSA.253...70B | s2cid= 53682417}}</ref> the effort to solve the RNase S 3-dimensional structure was spearheaded by Richards. Done in 1966 and published in 1967, the analyses of RNase S <ref name="rnaseS 3.5">{{cite journal| author=Wyckoff HW, Hardman KD, Allewell NM, Inagami T, [[Louise Johnson|Johnson LN]], Richards FM| title=The structure of ribonuclease-S at 3.5 Å resolution| year=1967| journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry| volume=242| issue=17| pages=3984–3988| pmid=6037556| title-link=angstrom| doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)95844-8| doi-access=free}}</ref> and RNase A<ref>{{cite journal| author=Kartha G, Bello J, [[David Harker|Harker D]]| journal=Nature |title=Tertiary Structure of Ribonuclease |volume=213 |year=1967 |pages=862–865 |doi=10.1038/213862a0 |pmid=6043657 |bibcode=1967Natur.213..862K |issue=5079| s2cid=4183721 }}</ref> jointly made ribonuclease the third distinct protein structure to be determined by [[X-ray diffraction]] of crystals, after [[myoglobin]]/[[hemoglobin]] and hen-egg [[lysozyme]],<ref>{{cite journal |author=Blake CCF, Koenig DF, Mair GA, North ACT, [[David Chilton Phillips|Phillips DC]], Sarma VR |year=1965 |title=Structure of hen egg-white lysozyme: a three-dimensional Fourier synthesis at 2 Å resolution |journal=Nature |volume=206 |pages=757–761 |doi=10.1038/206757a0 |bibcode=1965Natur.206..757B |issue=4986 |pmid=5891407|s2cid=4161467 }}</ref> and the first to be done in the United States. Later, the Yale group collected more diffraction data, and in 1970 published the RNase S structure in full detail at 2.0&nbsp;Å [[Resolution (electron density)|resolution]] ({{harvnb|Wyckoff et al., 1970}}). Coordinates for ribonuclease S were deposited into the international [[Protein Data Bank]] in 1973 as {{PDB|1RNS}}, among the first small set of macromolecular structures.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Bernstein FC, Koetzle T F, Williams, GJB, Meyer EF, Brice MD, Rodgers JR, [[Olga Kennard|Kennard O]], Shimanouchi T, Tasumi M |title=The protein data bank: A computer-based archival file for macromolecular structures |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |year=1977 |volume=112 |issue=3 |pages=535–542 |doi=10.1016/S0022-2836(77)80200-3 |pmid=875032}}</ref>

The black-and-white [[ribbon diagram|ribbon drawing]] above shows the large, twisted [[beta sheet]] (arrows) of ribonuclease, flanked by several [[alpha helix|alpha-helices]] (spirals). The shorter S-peptide piece is behind, starting at upper left with a helix and ending with the chain break (between residues 20-21) at lower right.<ref name="anatax"/> The active site for RNA cleavage (in the groove at center front in this drawing) involves one [[histidine]] side chain from the S-peptide fragment and another from the S-protein part.<ref name="rnaseS 3.5"/> The computer image shows superimposed structures of ribonuclease S and A, with the S-peptide in gold and the active site histidines in hot pink.  The close match of the 3D structures shows that the 2-fragment S system does indeed fold to the active form ({{harvnb|Wyckoff et al., 1970}}).

==="Richards' box"===
[[Image:Original Richards box photo.jpg|thumb|left| Original Richards box built by Richards in 1968 at Oxford]]

In 1968, while on sabbatical with [[David Chilton Phillips|David Phillips]] at Oxford, Richards developed a large [[optical comparator]] device called a "Richards' box" (or "Fred's Folly") which enabled crystallographers to build physical models of protein structures by viewing the stacked sheets of electron density through a [[half-silvered mirror]] (see photo).<ref name="Everts">{{cite journal|last1=Everts|first1=Sarah|title=Information Overload|journal=Distillations|date=2016|volume=2|issue=2|pages=26–33|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/distillations/magazine/information-overload|access-date=20 March 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author=Richards FM| title=The matching of physical models to three-dimensional electron-density maps: a simple optical device| journal= Journal of Molecular Biology| year=1968| volume=37| pages=225–230| pmid=5760491| issue=1| doi=10.1016/0022-2836(68)90085-5}}</ref> Once the Folly had been constructed, he built an all-atom brass model of RNase S quite rapidly.<ref name="Fred"/> This was the method of choice for building protein crystallographic models into electron density until the late 1970s, when it was superseded by [[molecular graphics|molecular computer graphics]] programs such as Grip-75<ref>{{cite journal |author=Brooks FP Jr |title=The Computer "Scientist" as Toolsmith: Studies in Interactive Computer Graphics |journal=Proceedings of IFIP (International Federation for Information Processing) Congress |year=1977 |pages=625–634 |publisher=North Holland|author-link=Frederick P. Brooks }}</ref> and then Frodo.<ref>{{cite journal| author=Jones TA |title=A Graphics Model Building and Refinement System for Macromolecules |year=1978 |journal=Journal of Applied Crystallography |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=268–272 |doi=10.1107/S0021889878013308|author-link=Alwyn Jones (biophysicist) |doi-access= |bibcode=1978JApCr..11..268J }}</ref>

Richards showed his sense of humor in a later review of developments in the use and construction of Richards boxes.<ref name="ME1985">{{cite book |author=Richards FM |title=Diffraction Methods for Biological Macromolecules Part B |chapter=Optical Matching of Physical Models and Electron Density Maps: Early Developments |year=1985 |series=Methods in Enzymology |volume=115 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/diffractionmetho0000unse/page/145 145–154] |doi=10.1016/0076-6879(85)15012-3 |pmid=3908881 |isbn=9780121820152 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/diffractionmetho0000unse/page/145 }}</ref> He provided a "correction to the Original Bibliographic Citations," complete with diagrams, for a theatrical stage technique that used selective illumination and a sheet of plate glass inclined at 45° to give an illusion of the nymph [[Amphitrite]] rising from the sea and floating in air, or of an audience volunteer dissolving to a skeleton and back again.  Richards ended that section by noting that "had this reference been known to the author in 1968 no further description of the 'folly' would have been required."<ref name="ME1985"/>

===Solvent-accessible surface and molecular packing===
Richards' most enduring long-term scientific interest was in [[protein folding]] and packing, studied both experimentally and theoretically, and mostly from a geometrical perspective.  As summarized by George Rose, "protein folders can be divided into 'minimizers' and 'packers'. The former seek to minimize the interaction energy among atoms or groups of atoms, whereas the latter concentrate on probable geometry, guided by both excluded volume limitations and structural motifs seen in proteins of known structure." Fred was a founding influence for the packers, who built on his observations about packing density, areas, and volumes.<ref name="Rose"/>

[[Image:Surfacetype Solvent-Accessible.png|thumb|right|Diagram showing definition of [[Solvent Accessible Surface]] (SAS), in yellow dots]]
In 1971, with Byungkook Lee, Richards introduced the concept and a quantitative measure for the [[solvent-accessible surface]] (SAS) of [[amino acid]] residues in folded protein structures ({{harvnb|Lee|Richards|1971}}). The surface is constructed by tracing the center of an imaginary ball, its radius that of a water molecule (taken as 1.4&nbsp;Å), as it rolls over the [[van der Waals surface]]s of the proteins. Thus defined, the surface is continuous and each point on it is unambiguously associated with a specific protein atom (the nearest). The Lee & Richards definition has been widely adopted as the standard measure for solvent accessibility, for instance to evaluate exposure per residue as a percentage of accessible vs total surface area,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Shrake A, Rupley JA |year=1973 |title=Environment and exposure to solvent of protein atoms. Lysozyme and insulin |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |volume=79 |pages=351–71 |doi= 10.1016/0022-2836(73)90011-9 |pmid=4760134 |issue=2}}</ref> and as the basis of the buried-surface-area method for estimating the energetics of protein/protein contacts.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Chothia C |title=The nature of the accessible and buried surfaces in proteins |year=1976 |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |volume=105 |pages=1–12 |pmid=994183 |doi=10.1016/0022-2836(76)90191-1 |issue=1}}</ref>

{{harvnb|Richards|1974}} introduced the [[Voronoi diagram|Voronoi polyhedra]] construction to protein chemistry, a contribution reviewed more recently by Gerstein and Richards.<ref>{{cite book |author1=M Gerstein |author2=F M Richards |journal=International Tables for Crystallography |volume=F |pages= 531–539 |year=2001 |title=Protein Geometry: volumes, areas, and distances.|doi=10.1107/97809553602060000710 |isbn=978-0-7923-6857-1 }}</ref> This approach has been adopted by many others<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Gerstein M, Tsai J, Levitt M |year=1995 |title=The volume of atoms on the protein surface: calculated from simulation, using Voronoi polyhedra |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |volume=249 |pages=955–966 |doi=10.1006/jmbi.1995.0351 |pmid=7540695 |issue=5|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Poupon A |title=Voronoi and Voronoi-related tessellations in studies of protein structure and interaction |journal=Current Opinion in Structural Biology |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=233–41 |year=2004 |doi=10.1016/j.sbi.2004.03.010 |pmid=15093839|s2cid=6952862 }}</ref> and has been put on a firm mathematical footing by the work of [[Herbert Edelsbrunner]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Edelsbrunner H, Mucke EP |title=Three-dimensional alpha shapes |year=1994 |journal=ACM Transactions on Graphics |volume=13 |pages=43–72 |doi=10.1145/174462.156635|arxiv=math/9410208 |bibcode=1994math.....10208E |s2cid=1600979 }}</ref>
With Jay Ponder in 1987, as part of an exploration of using internal packing of sidechains to enumerate the possible sequences compatible with a given protein backbone structure (a foreshadowing of protein engineering and design), Richards developed the first side-chain [[rotamer]] library. ({{harvnb|Ponder|Richards|1987}}) Increasingly detailed rotamer libraries, such as the [[Backbone-dependent rotamer library]], have been made since then by other research groups, with some used primarily for [[structure validation]]<ref>{{cite journal|author=Read RJ, Adams PD, Arendall WB III, Brunger AT, Emsley P, Joosten RP, Kleywegt GJ, Krissinel EB, Lütteke T, Otwinowski Z, Perrakis A, [[Jane S. Richardson|Richardson JS]], Sheffler WH, Smith JL, Tickle IJ, Vriend G, Zwart PH|title=A New Generation of Crystallographic Validation Tools for the Protein Data Bank |journal=Structure |year=2011 |volume=19 |issue=10 |pages=1395–1412 |doi=10.1016/j.str.2011.08.006 |pmc=3195755 |pmid=22000512}}</ref> and others for [[homology modeling]] or [[protein design]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=Dunbrack RL Jr. |title=Rotamer libraries in the 21st century |year=2002 |journal=Current Opinion in Structural Biology |volume=12 |pages=431–40 |pmid=12163064 |doi=10.1016/S0959-440X(02)00344-5 |issue=4}}</ref>
With Craig Kundrot, Richards investigated the effects of high pressure (1000 [[Atmosphere (unit)|atmosphere]]s) on protein structure, using hen-egg [[lysozyme]] crystals,<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Kundrot CE, Richards FM | title=Crystal structure of hen egg-white lysozyme at a hydrostatic pressure of 1000 atmospheres| year=1987| journal=Journal of Molecular Biology| volume=193| issue=1| pages=157–170 |doi=10.1016/0022-2836(87)90634-6| pmid=3586017| doi-access=free}}</ref> finding that the structure was robust to such pressures apart from a quite modest compaction in size. In the 1990s, Richards and collaborators used a combination of theory and experiment to investigate how the well-packed interior of proteins can nevertheless accommodate [[mutation]]s.<ref>{{cite journal| author=Varadarajan R, Richards, FM| title=Crystallographic structures of ribonuclease S variants with nonpolar substitution at position 13: packing and cavities| year=1992| journal=Biochemistry| volume=31| pages=12315–12327 |pmid=1463720| issue=49| doi=10.1021/bi00164a005}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Lim WA, Hodel A, Sauer RT, Richards FM | title=The crystal structure of a mutant protein with altered but improved hydrophobic core packing| year=1994|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America| volume= 91| pages=423–427| pmid=8278404 |pmc=42960| issue=1|bibcode = 1994PNAS...91..423L |doi = 10.1073/pnas.91.1.423 | doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Wynn R, Harkins PC, Richards FM, Fox RO | title=Mobile unnatural amino acid side chains in the core of staphylococcal nuclease| year=1996| journal=Protein Science |volume=5| pages=1026–1031 |pmc=2143447| pmid=8762134| doi=10.1002/pro.5560050605| issue=6}}</ref>

===Other research areas===
In the 1970s, with a succession of students and postdocs, the lab developed a series of chemical,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Kuan |last2=Richards |first2=Frederic M. |date=December 1974 |title=An Approach to Nearest Neighbor Analysis of Membrane Proteins |journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=249 |issue=24 |pages=8005–8018 |doi=10.1016/s0021-9258(19)42065-6 |issn=0021-9258|doi-access=free }}</ref> [[photochemistry|photochemical]],<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Staros JV, Richards FM |year=1974 |title=Photochemical labeling of the surface proteins of human erythrocytes |journal=Biochemistry |volume=13 |issue=13 |pages=2720–2726 |doi=10.1021/bi00710a010 |pmid=4847541}}</ref> and cross-link labels for determining the position and relationships of proteins in [[biological membranes]] ({{harvnb|Peters|Richards|1977}}), including [[glutaraldehyde]]<ref>{{cite journal |author=Richards FM, [[Jeremy R. Knowles|Knowles JR]] |title=Glutaraldehyde as a protein cross-linking reagent |year=1968 |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=231–233 |doi=10.1016/0022-2836(68)90086-7|pmid=5760492 }}</ref> and what was one of the two first general uses of the exceptionally tight interaction of [[biotin]] with [[avidin]],<ref name="Fred"/> anchored to [[ferritin]] for use in [[electron microscopy]].<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Heitzmann H, Richards FM | year=1974| title=Use of the avidin–biotin complex for specific staining of biological membranes in electron microscopy| journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America| volume=71| pages=3537–3541 |pmc=433809| pmid=4139715| issue=9|bibcode = 1974PNAS...71.3537H |doi = 10.1073/pnas.71.9.3537 | doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author1=Manning, J. E. |author2=Hershey, N. D. |author3=Broker, T. R. |author4=Pellegrini, M. |author5=Mitchell, H. K. |author6=Davidson, N. |title=A new method of in situ hybridization |year=1975 |journal=Chromosoma |volume=53 |pages=107–117 |pmid=172297 |issue=2 |doi=10.1007/bf00333039|s2cid=29595419 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Richards FM |title=Reflections |chapter=&#91;1&#93; Reflections |year=1990 |series=Methods in Enzymology |volume=184 |pages=3–5 |doi=10.1016/0076-6879(90)84255-F |pmid=2201877|isbn=9780121820855 }}</ref>  The biotin–avidin system quickly became a central method in cell biology, immunology, and protein engineering, as well as electron microscopy.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Diamandis EP, Christopoulos TK |title=The biotin-(strept)avidin system: principles and applications in biotechnology |year=1991 |journal=Clinical Chemistry |volume=37 |pages=625–636 |pmid=2032315 |issue=5|doi=10.1093/clinchem/37.5.625 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

With David Wishart and Brian Sykes, he developed the [[chemical shift]] index for NMR assignment of protein [[secondary structure]] ({{harvnb|Wishart|Sykes|Richards|1991}} & {{harvnb|Wishart|Sykes|Richards|1992}}).  This is still considered a standard tool in the NMR field.<ref>{{Cite book |author1=Cavanagh, John |author2=Fairbrother, Wayne J. |author3=Palmer, Arthur G. III |author4=Skelton, Nicholas J. |title=Protein NMR Spectroscopy: Principles and Practice |edition=2nd |year=2006 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-12-164491-8 |ref={{harvid|Cavanagh|2006}} }}</ref>  Separately, around 1990, Homme Hellinga, with Richards, developed computational tools to [[protein design|design]] metal-binding sites into proteins,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Hellinga HW, Richards FM |title=Construction of new ligand-binding sites in proteins of known structure.1. Computer-aided modeling of sites with predefined geometry |year=1991 |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |volume=222 |issue=3 |pages=763–785 |doi=10.1016/0022-2836(91)90510-D|pmid=1749000 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and used them to build a new metal site into [[thioredoxin]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Hellinga HW, Carradona JP, Richards FM |title=Construction of new ligand-binding sites in proteins of known structure. 2. Grafting of a buried transition-metal binding site into E coli thioredoxin |year=1991 |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |volume=222 |issue=3 |pages=787–803 |doi=10.1016/0022-2836(91)90511-4|pmid=1660933 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Richards is named as a depositor on 27 crystal structure entries in the [[Protein Data Bank]], including the now-obsoleted ribonuclease S ({{PDB|1RNS}}), hen egg [[lysozyme]] ({{PDB|2LYM}}), [[SH3 domain]]s ({{PDB|1SEM}}), the [[ion channel|ion-channel-forming]] [[alamethicin]] ({{PDB|1AMT}}) ({{harvnb|Fox|Richards|1982}}), and [[mutant]]s of ribonuclease S (e.g., {{PDB|1RBD}};{{PDB|1RBI}}), of [[Staphylococcus|Staphylococcal]] [[nuclease]] (e.g., {{PDB|1NUC}};{{PDB|1A2T}}), and of lambda repressor in complex with [[DNA]] ({{PDB|1LLI}}).

==Administration, mentoring, and outside activities==
The Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry ("MB&B")<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.mbb.yale.edu/ |title=Welcome &#124; Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry |access-date=2012-06-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216030934/https://mbb.yale.edu/ |archive-date=2019-02-16 |url-status=dead }}</ref> that Richards founded and chaired at Yale, which amalgamated the medical school Biochemistry and the university Molecular Biophysics departments, was considered to have "quickly gained pre-eminent stature."<ref name="Rose"/> Many of those faculty became members of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]],<ref name="Steitz"/><ref name="Rose"/> and [[Thomas Steitz|Tom Steitz]] shared the [[Nobel Prize]] in 2009 for crystal structures of the ribosome.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/2009/ |title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2009|publisher=Nobelprize.org|access-date=21 May 2012}}</ref> Richards was known as a highly valued mentor and friend to students, faculty, and colleagues, including a very supportive approach to women and African–Americans, according to Norma Allewell, quoted in a remembrance by Jim Staros.<ref name="Staros">{{cite journal| author=Staros JV| title=Retrospective: Frederic M. Richards (1925–2009)| journal=ASBMB Today| volume=April 2009| pages=16–18| url=http://www.asbmb.org/uploadedFiles/AboutUs/ASBMB_History/200904Frederic%20Richards%20-%20April%202009.pdf| access-date=2012-06-19| archive-date=2012-06-03| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120603130420/http://www.asbmb.org/uploadedFiles/AboutUs/ASBMB_History/200904Frederic%20Richards%20-%20April%202009.pdf| url-status=dead}}</ref> His colleague George D. Rose wrote that Richards' lectures were insightful, delivered with clarity and humor, and often deliberately provocative, and that Richards worked to improve the scientific community in general.<ref name="Rose"/> For instance, in the late 1980s, he was the primary author, and the first of many signers, of a widely circulated letter that successfully urged a policy of depositing 3D atomic coordinates on scientific journals, on the [[National Institutes of Health|NIH]], and on individual crystallographers.<ref name="Fred"/><ref>{{cite journal |author=Richards FM |title=Public access to x-ray diffraction data |year=1988 |journal=Journal of Computer-Aided Molecular Design |volume=2 |pages=3–4 |doi=10.1007/BF01532048 |pmid=3199147 |issue=1|bibcode = 1988JCAMD...2....3R |s2cid=6084669 }}</ref> He also lobbied, less successfully, for a let-up in overall publication pressure but an increased emphasis on a few first-class papers, by having promotion committees only consider a list of 12 key papers.<ref name="Fred"/>

==Summary of career events==
* 1954, NRC Postdoctoral Fellow, [[Carlsberg Laboratory]], Denmark<ref name="Carlsberg">{{cite journal | author=Richards FM| year=1992| title=Linderstrøm-Lang and the Carlsberg Laboratory: the view of a postdoctoral fellow in 1954| journal=Protein Science |volume=1| issue=12| pages=1721–1730 |doi=10.1002/pro.5560011221 |pmc=2142135 | pmid=1304902}}</ref>
* 1955, joined [[Yale University|Yale]] faculty, in Biochemistry at the Medical School<ref name="Staros"/>
* 1963, Professor and chair of the Department of Molecular Biophysics at Yale University<ref name="Fred"/>
* 1965, [[Pfizer]] – [[Paul-Lewis Award in Enzyme Chemistry]]
* 1968, Member, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]<ref>{{cite book|chapter-url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterR.pdf |title=Members of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences: 1780&ndash;2011 |chapter=R |page=500 |publisher=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |year=2012 }}</ref>
* 1969–73, founding chair of the Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry at Yale<ref name="Fred"/>
* 1971, Member, [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Frederic M. Richards |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/frederic-m-richards-6kgmqq/ |access-date=2022-04-01 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref>
* 1972, President of the [[Biophysical Society]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.biophysics.org/AboutUs/Leadership/PastOfficers/tabid/2241/Default.aspx |title=Past Officers |publisher=Biophysical Society |access-date=19 June 2012}}</ref>
* 1976–91, Director of the Jane Coffin Childs Fund for Medical Research<ref name="Fred"/>
* 1978, Kaj Linderstrøm-Lang Prize in Protein Chemistry
* 1979, President of the [[American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology|ASBMB]]<ref name="Staros"/>
* 1988, American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology – [[Merck & Co.|Merck]] Award <ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.asbmb.org/Page.aspx?id=508 |title=ASBMB-Merck Award |publisher=ASBMB |access-date=18 June 2012 |archive-date=2 October 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161002024623/http://www.asbmb.org/Page.aspx?id=508 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* 1988, Protein Society – Stein and Moore Award <ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.proteinsociety.org/pages/page03b.htm |publisher=Protein Society |title=Past award recipients |access-date=18 June 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080513115337/http://www.proteinsociety.org/pages/page03b.htm |archive-date=13 May 2008 }}</ref>
* 1992, Member, [[American Philosophical Society]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Frederic+M.+Richards&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=2022-04-01 |website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref>
* 1995, Connecticut Medal of Science<ref name="Steitz"/>
